title: India to Pitch RBI-Backed Digital Currency Link for BRICS Payments at Summit
excerpt: New Delhi will push its proposal to link BRICS central bank digital currencies at the leaders' summit on September 12-13, according to Reuters — but low adoption and political frictions cloud its prospects.
body:
• India will put the RBI's proposal to link BRICS central bank digital currencies for cross-border payments on the agenda of the leaders' summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, according to two sources cited by Reuters.
  • The plan builds on a 2025 Rio declaration calling for interoperability between BRICS members' payment systems; the RBI first recommended it to the government in January.
  • Hurdles include low CBDC adoption globally, members' reluctance to use each other's technology platforms, and political strains such as Iran–UAE tensions.
  • At home, the e-rupee has grown to about 10 million users with $3.6 billion in cumulative transactions, and the RBI is routing welfare payments through it to drive usage.

India will push a proposal to link central bank digital currencies across BRICS nations for cross-border payments when the bloc's leaders meet in New Delhi on September 12–13, according to Reuters, which cited two sources familiar with the discussions. The Reserve Bank of India, which authored the plan, wants the official digital currencies of member states connected to ease trade and tourism payments across the 11-member group.

Reuters said the sources spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to talk to the media, and that emails to India's external affairs and finance ministries and to the RBI went unanswered.

A proposal that has been taking shape all year

The push is not new. The RBI recommended to the government in January that linking BRICS digital currencies be placed on the summit agenda, in a proposal first reported by Reuters at the time. The idea builds on a declaration adopted at the 2025 BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro, which called for interoperability between members' payment systems to make cross-border transactions more efficient.

The RBI has publicly expressed interest in linking India's digital rupee with other nations' CBDCs to expedite cross-border transactions and strengthen the rupee's global usage. It has, however, said its efforts are not aimed at promoting de-dollarisation — a sensitive point given that U.S. President Donald Trump has called BRICS "anti-American" and threatened tariffs on its members.

"The RBI has publicly expressed interest in linking India's digital rupee with other nations' CBDCs to expedite cross-border transactions and bolster its currency's global usage."

— Reuters, reporting on the RBI's stated position

Technical and political headwinds

Even with India's chairmanship of the bloc this year, the proposal faces steep obstacles. None of the BRICS members has fully launched a digital currency — all are still running pilots — and limited global adoption could complicate implementation.

One source told Reuters that hesitation among members to adopt technological platforms from other countries could hinder work on the proposal, and that consensus on technology and regulation would be needed for any real progress. Strained relations within the bloc, such as between Iran and the UAE — the latter has cut financial ties with Tehran — will remain a sticking point.

Trade imbalances pose another problem. Previous attempts by Russia and India to settle more trade in local currencies stumbled when Russia accumulated large rupee balances it could barely use, prompting the RBI to let them be invested in Indian bonds. One idea under discussion to manage imbalances in a CBDC network is bilateral foreign exchange swap arrangements between central banks.

India's domestic e-rupee experiment

India is simultaneously trying to prove out the use case at home. The e-rupee, launched in December 2022, has about 10 million users, but cumulative transactions total just $3.6 billion — modest next to the Unified Payments Interface, which processes roughly $300 billion each month.

To build usage, the RBI is running about 10 pilot programs routing portions of India's roughly $80 billion welfare system through the e-rupee, according to Reuters reporting in April. In Maharashtra's Phulenagar village, farmers get programmable subsidies covering up to 80% of drip-irrigation costs, spendable only at approved vendors. A Gujarat pilot aims to onboard all 7.5 million eligible food-subsidy households by June. The pilots are designed to cut leakage in subsidy programs while giving the CBDC a concrete job to do.

What it means for Indians abroad

A working CBDC link could eventually lower the cost and settlement time of cross-border payments between India and other BRICS economies — including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, home to millions of Indian workers whose remittances flow through correspondent banking chains today. It would also give Indian exporters an alternative rail for trade with Russia, Brazil and South Africa that does not depend on the dollar. Both outcomes, however, hinge on adoption that remains years away.

What to watch

The September 12–13 summit will show whether India's chairmanship can convert a recommendation into a work plan — requiring agreement on interoperable technology, governance rules, and settling imbalanced trade volumes, none of which earlier BRICS talks on shared payment mechanisms achieved. Reuters notes those discussions "made little headway."
